source_text: Iam enim et in ista specie ditati saturatique regnatis, non delicta incursantes, quae ieiuniis elimentur, nec reuelationum scientia indigentes, quae xerophagiis extorqueantur, nec bella propria metuentes, quae stationibus discutiantur. ut ab Iohanne paracletus obmutuisset, et ipsi nobis prophetae in hanc maxime causam extitissemus, iam non dico ad exorandam dei iram nec ad impetrandam tutelam eius aut gratiam, sed ad praemuniendam per nosmet ipsos nouissimorum temporum condicionem indicentes omnem Tonueivoippovrjariv, cum carcer ediscendus et fames ac sitis exercendae et tam inediae quam anxii uictus tolerantia usurpanda sit, ut in carcerem talis introeat Christianus, qualis inde prodisset, non poenam illic passurus, sed disciplinam, nec saeculi tormenta, sed sua officia, eoque fidentior processurus ad certamen e custodia abusus nihil habens carnis, sic ut nec habeant tormenta materiam, cum sola et arida sit cute loricatus, et contra ungulas corneus, praemisso iam sanguinis suco tamquam animae impedimentis, properante iam et ipsa, quae iam saepe ieiunans mortem de proximo norit. plane uestrum est in carceribus popinas exhibere martyribus incertis, ne consuetudinem quaerant, ne taedeat uitae, ne noua abstinentiae disciplina scandalizentur, quam nec ille Pristinus uester non Christianus martyr adtigerat, quem ex facultate custodiae liberae aliquamdiu fartum, omnibus balneis quasi baptismate melioribus et omnibus luxuriae secessibus quasi ecclesia secretioribus et omnibus uitae istius inlecebris quasi aeterna dignioribus hoc puto obligatum mori uellet, postremo ipso tribunalis die luce summa condito mero tamquam antidoto praemedicatum ita eneruastis, ut paucis ungulis titillatus (hoc enim ebrietas sentiebat) quem dominum confiteretur interroganti praesidi respondere non potuerit amplius, atque ita de hoc iam extortus, cum singultus et ructus solos haberet, in ipsa negatione discessit. ideo sobrietatis disciplinam qui praedicant, pseudoprophetae, ideo haeretici, qui obseruant. quid ergo cessatis paracletum, quem in Montano negatis, in Apicio credere?
thought_title: The belly's reign and the martyr's discipline
orientation: Tertullian is attacking his opponents for being rich and full-fed, and contrasting their pampered martyr Pristinus with the fasting discipline that prepares a Christian for prison and torture.
pass_a_gloss: For now also in this very condition, enriched and sated, you reign, not running against the offenses which are eliminated by fasts, nor needing the knowledge of revelations which are extorted by dry-food fasts, nor fearing your own wars which are scattered by station fasts. So that the Advocate had become mute from John, and we ourselves would have become prophets to you for this very great cause, no longer I say for appeasing the wrath of God nor for obtaining his protection or grace, but for fortifying through ourselves the condition of the newest times, imposing every self-control, since prison must be learned and hunger and thirst must be practiced and the endurance both of fasting and of anxious sustenance must be taken up, so that such a Christian enters into prison as he would come out from there, not about to suffer punishment there, but discipline, nor the torments of the world, but his own duties, and by this more confident about to go forth to the contest from custody, having abused nothing of the flesh, so that torments do not have material, since he is armored with skin alone and dry, and horny against the claws, the juice of his blood having already been sent ahead as hindrances of the soul, and she herself already hastening, who already often fasting has known death from nearby. Clearly it is yours to exhibit cook-shops in prisons to uncertain martyrs, lest they seek habit, lest life weary them, lest they be scandalized by the new discipline of abstinence, which not even that Pristinus of yours, a non-Christian martyr, had touched, whom, stuffed for some time by the opportunity of free custody, with all baths as if better than baptism and all retreats of luxury as if more secret than the church and all enticements of this life as if more worthy than eternal things, you wanted to die bound by this, I think; finally on the very day of the tribunal, in full daylight, having been pre-medicated with pure wine as if with an antidote, you so enervated him that, tickled by a few claws (for this drunkenness felt), he could not answer more to the governor asking which lord he confessed, and so already extorted from this, since he had only hiccups and belches, he departed in the very denial. Therefore those who preach the discipline of sobriety are false prophets, therefore heretics, who observe it. Why then do you delay to believe in the Advocate, whom you deny in Montanus, in Apicius?

choices.why: The source text is corrupt here; the context and the glossary term continentia (self-control) make this the intended sense. I render the damaged word as 'self-control' and flag the corruption in notes.
The glossary requires 'station fasts' for stationes, the Wednesday and Friday fasts.
The glossary requires 'dry-food fasts' for xerophagiae.
The glossary requires 'the Advocate' for paracletus, the Holy Spirit.
Popina means a low-class eating-house or cook-shop; the literal sense conveys the pampering of prisoners with food.
Apicius is the famous glutton; the name is kept as a proper noun, with the point that they believe in a glutton as their 'advocate'.

pass_b_english: For now, enriched and sated, you reign even in this kind of thing. You do not run against sins that fasting eliminates, nor do you need the knowledge of revelations that dry-food fasts extort, nor do you fear your own wars that station fasts scatter. So the Advocate would have fallen silent after John, and we ourselves would have become prophets for this very purpose—I no longer say to appease God's wrath or to obtain his protection or grace, but to fortify in advance through our own efforts the condition of the last times by proclaiming every form of self-control. Prison must be learned, hunger and thirst must be practiced, and endurance of both fasting and anxious diet must be made our own, so that a Christian enters prison the same kind of person he will come out—not about to suffer punishment there, but discipline; not the torments of the world, but his own duties. And he will go out to the contest all the more confident, having used his custody well, possessing nothing of the flesh, so that torments have no material to work on, since he is armored with skin alone, dry and horny against the claws, having already drained the blood that weighs down the soul, and the soul itself now hurrying on, since by frequent fasting it has already learned death from close at hand.

Clearly it is your way to provide cook-shops in prisons for uncertain martyrs, so they do not seek out the old habit, so they do not grow tired of life, so they are not scandalized by the new discipline of self-control. Not even your Pristinus, a non-Christian martyr, had touched that discipline. You had stuffed him for some time thanks to the freedom of his open custody, with all the baths as if better than baptism, all the retreats of luxury as if more secluded than the church, all the enticements of this life as if more worthy than eternal things—bound by all this, I think, he wanted to die. Finally, on the very day of his trial, in broad daylight, you medicated him in advance with unmixed wine as if with an antidote, and so enervated him that, scratched by a few claws (for this is what drunkenness felt), he could not answer the governor who asked him what lord he confessed, and so, already wrung out from this, having only hiccups and belches, he departed in the very act of denial. Therefore those who preach the discipline of sobriety are false prophets; therefore those who observe it are heretics. So why do you hesitate to believe in the Advocate whom you deny in Montanus, but believe in Apicius?
notes: The word 'Tonueivoippovrjariv' is corrupt in the source. It appears to be a garbled form of a Greek term for self-control (likely ἐγκράτειαν or similar), and the context supports 'self-control' as the sense. The gloss renders it as 'self-control' but the corruption is noted here.

last_rejected.quote: and the soul itself now hurrying on, since by frequent fasting it has already learned death from close at hand
last_rejected.source_quote: properante iam et ipsa, quae iam saepe ieiunans mortem de proximo norit
last_rejected.why: Subject is the blood/juice, not the soul; 'animae impedimentis' means 'as impediments to the soul', and 'norit' = 'has come to know'.
last_rejected.fix: with the soul's own impediments now hurrying on too, since by frequent fasting it has already come to know death from close at hand.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'ipsa' refers to 'anima' (soul); translation correctly links soul hurrying and knowing death.

last_rejected.quote: having already sent ahead the juice of his blood as a hindrance to the soul
last_rejected.source_quote: praemisso iam sanguinis suco tamquam animae impedimentis
last_rejected.why: 'sanguinis suco' is the subject of 'praemisso'; it means the blood's moisture/juice has been sent ahead as impediments to the soul, not 'his blood's juice as a hindrance to the soul'.
last_rejected.fix: having already sent ahead the blood's moisture as impediments to the soul
last_rejected.ruling: 'praemisso ... sanguinis suco tamquam animae impedimentis' = blood juice sent as impediment to soul; translation matches.

last_rejected.quote: nor do you fear your own wars that station fasts scatter
last_rejected.source_quote: nec bella propria metuentes, quae stationibus discutiantur
last_rejected.why: Latin says wars are examined/settled by stations; English says they are scattered, changing the meaning.
last_rejected.fix: nor do you fear your own wars that are examined by station fasts
last_rejected.ruling: discutiantur can mean 'scatter/dispel'; 'wars scattered by stations' is within normal range, not a major error.

problems.why: Same Montanist title for Holy Spirit rendered differently; reader may miss connections.

variants.text: the advocate for entreating the judge

problems.why: Movement name vs. opponents' accusation of 'false prophecy' may confuse reader about whether these are same or different.
problems.fix: Clarify 'New Prophecy' is movement name; opponents call it 'false prophecy'.

problems.quote: Therefore those who preach the discipline of sobriety are false prophets; therefore those who observe it are heretics. So why do you hesitate to believe in the Advocate whom you deny in Montanus, but believe in Apicius?
problems.why: Sarcastic voice shift from opponents' accusation to Tertullian's counter unclear.
problems.fix: Clarify these are opponents' claims Tertullian is mocking.

problems.quote: having already sent ahead the juice of his blood as a hindrance to the soul
problems.why: Physiological/metaphorical claim unclear; how is blood-juice a hindrance?
Mistranslation or too literal; should be 'scratched' or 'torn by claws' in martyrdom.
Advocate (Paraclete) and Holy Spirit are the same entity; reader may not connect them.
problems.fix: Clarify early that 'the Advocate' is the Holy Spirit/Paraclete.

problems.quote: having already sent ahead the juice of his blood as a hindrance to the soul
problems.why: Metaphor is opaque; 'hindrance' seems wrong for the argument.
problems.fix: Rephrase: 'having already drained the blood that weighs down the soul.'

fixed: Glossary 'the Advocate': The brief's glossary already mandates 'the Advocate' for paracletus, and the English uses it consistently. No edit needed.
Glossary 'New Prophecy': The brief's glossary already mandates 'the New Prophecy' for noua prophetia. The English does not use the term in this section, so no edit is needed.

Speaker: The sarcastic voice shift is already clear in the English: 'Therefore those who preach... are false prophets; therefore those who observe it are heretics' is followed by Tertullian's counter-question 'So why do you hesitate...'. No edit needed.

Unreadable 'juice of his blood': The source reads 'praemisso iam sanguinis suco tamquam animae impedimentis' — the blood's juice is sent ahead as hindrances of the soul. The English 'as a hindrance to the soul' misstates the plural and the sense; the blood is what hinders the soul, so 'drained the blood that weighs down the soul' better captures the argument. Edited.

Mistranslation 'tickled by a few claws': The source 'paucis ungulis titillatus' uses titillatus, which can mean 'tickled', but in the context of martyrdom claws (ungulae) tearing flesh, 'scratched' better conveys the physical torment. Edited.
Glossary 'the Advocate': Already addressed above; the brief mandates 'the Advocate' and the English uses it. No edit needed.
Unreadable 'juice of his blood': Already addressed above; edited to 'drained the blood that weighs down the soul'.
